metadata.title: Motivational components in TIMSS 2015 and their effects on engaging teaching practices and mathematics performance

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2015 Student Context Questionnaire (SCQ) data for the United States, with a two-stage stratified cluster sampling design (schools sampled with probability proportional to size, then intact classes sampled within schools). Although the authors discuss that sample weights are often used in design-based approaches, they explicitly state that a model-based approach was applied and therefore sample weights were not taken into consideration. Analyses were conducted separately for eighth-grade SCQ and then repeated with fourth-grade SCQ. Data screening retained outliers (rather than deleting them) and the authors used the TIMSS plausible value methodology for mathematics achievement as the dependent variable.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper reports item-level missingness rates (≤4.8% for grade 4 and ≤3.2% for grade 8) but does not specify the exact missing-data handling method used in the SEM estimation (e.g., whether missing responses were handled via full-information methods, listwise deletion, or another approach). Because the dependent variable is based on TIMSS plausible values and the authors do not document the missing-response treatment, the missing-data strategy cannot be verified from the provided text. This is a reporting gap for reproducibility.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2015 administration data for the United States only (publicly available). Included students in the target grades (fourth and eighth) who completed the Student Context Questionnaire (SCQ) after the mathematics achievement assessment. The study reports that students with functional/intellectual disabilities and non-native speakers could be excluded per TIMSS guidelines (with exclusions not exceeding 5% of the national target population), and it retained outliers rather than deleting or recoding them. No additional analytic exclusions beyond the TIMSS sampling framework and the SEM/PV workflow are described.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2015 Grade 8 Mathematics (USA) — Student Context Questionnaire (SCQ) latent model with plausible values
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM (CFA/SEM with Mplus WLSMV). Model fit: CFI=0.945, RMSEA=0.075, SRMR=0.061 (Model 1.5). Predictive paths: ET→E β=0.588 (p<.001), E explained variance=34.5%; E→performance β=-0.331 (p<.001); SC→performance β=0.785 (p<.001); IU→performance β=0.078 (p<.001); ET→performance β=-0.107 (p<.001). Attitude predictors explained 30.2% of performance variance. Mediation: total ET→performance β=-0.301 (p<.001), direct ET→performance β=-0.107 (p<.001), indirect via enjoyment β=-0.195 (p<.001) with 99% CI reported for PV1.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2015 Grade 8 Mathematics (USA) the study leveraged self-concept in mathematics, engaging teaching behavior, enjoyment of mathematics, and importance and usefulness (math) to predict mathematics performance (plausible values), finding that self-concept had the strongest positive association with performance while engaging teaching and enjoyment showed negative predictive coefficients after accounting for self-concept. This indicates that reforms aiming to raise students’ mathematics self-confidence may be more effective for achievement than focusing solely on perceived enjoyment or teacher engagement, though the negative coefficients should be interpreted as conditional associations within the multivariate SEM rather than standalone effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2015 Grade 4 Mathematics (USA) — Student Context Questionnaire (SCQ) latent model with plausible values
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM (CFA/SEM with Mplus WLSMV). Model fit: CFI=0.962, RMSEA=0.064, SRMR=0.058 (Model 2.5). Predictive paths: ET→E β=0.593 (p<.001), E explained variance=35.2%; E→performance β=-0.467 (p<.001); SC→performance β=0.881 (p<.001); ET→performance β=-0.050 (p=.002). Motivational factors plus ET explained 37.6% of performance variance. Mediation: total ET→performance β=-0.327 (p<.001), direct ET→performance β=-0.050 (p=.002), indirect via enjoyment β=-0.277 (p<.001) with 99% CI reported for PV1.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2015 Grade 4 Mathematics (USA) the study leveraged self-concept in mathematics, engaging teaching behavior, and enjoyment of mathematics to predict mathematics performance (plausible values), finding that self-concept was strongly and positively associated with performance while enjoyment and engaging teaching had negative predictive effects after controlling for self-concept. This indicates that early-grade mathematics interventions should prioritize building students’ expectancy of success (self-concept), while teacher engagement strategies may need careful alignment with how they translate into effective learning experiences rather than only increasing reported enjoyment.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes TIMSS 2015 Student Context Questionnaire (SCQ) data from the United States for both fourth and eighth grades, modeling motivational constructs (enjoyment, self-concept, and importance/usefulness where available) and engaging teaching as latent factors. Mathematics achievement is the dependent variable, estimated using TIMSS plausible values; the authors enter all five plausible values simultaneously in the SEM and report model fit using CFI, RMSEA, and SRMR under the WLSMV estimator. For Grade 8, the structural model fit was adequate (CFI=0.945, RMSEA=0.075, SRMR=0.061) and self-concept strongly predicted performance (β=0.785, p<.001), while enjoyment and engaging teaching showed negative conditional effects (E→β=-0.331; ET→β=-0.107). For Grade 4, fit was also adequate (CFI=0.962, RMSEA=0.064, SRMR=0.058) with an even stronger self-concept effect (β=0.881, p<.001) and negative conditional effects for enjoyment (β=-0.467) and engaging teaching (β=-0.050). The study explicitly does not apply sampling weights (model-based approach) and uses cross-sectional SEM, so the mediation results do not establish causal direction.
